title: What’s behind this summer’s heat, and why 2027 could be worse
gist: MIT Technology Review's climate newsletter explains that record 2026 heat across Europe, the contiguous US and South Korea came largely from long-term warming, while the newly arrived El Niño — possibly the strongest on record, with one of the fastest onsets ever observed — has yet to deliver most of its effect. Because El Niño's temperature impact lags by several months and historically peaks in the event's second calendar year (2023's event made 2024 the hottest year on record), the author expects 2027 to be hotter than 2026 and advises buying cooling, solar-plus-battery and insulation now.

insights.claim: June and July 2026 were the hottest two-month stretch in Europe since record-keeping began, the contiguous US had its hottest month on record in July, and South Korea set its highest-ever recorded temperature.
insights.so_what: Simultaneous multi-region records establish the baseline against which 2027 is being forecast higher — relevant to power demand, crop and insurance loss models.
insights.quote: June and July marked the hottest two-month stretch in Europe since record-keeping began. The contiguous US endured its hottest month on record in July. South Korea saw its highest-ever recorded temperature.
insights.locator: This summer has been a scorcher
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: July 2026 broke a contiguous-US heat record held by July 1936 for nearly a century, meaning Dust Bowl-era extremes are now being exceeded.
insights.so_what: Breaking Dust Bowl benchmarks resets the tail assumptions in US agricultural and grid stress models built on 20th-century maxima.
insights.quote: July’s record for the contiguous US (which excludes Alaska and Hawaii) officially ends one held by July 1936 for nearly a century.
insights.locator: The US hasn’t been excused from the heat either
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, second only to the Arctic in regional warming rate, which explains its disproportionate heat wave burden.
insights.so_what: Regional warming asymmetry argues for European overweight in cooling demand, grid stress and heat-adaptation exposure relative to global averages.
insights.quote: But different regions see different warming rates, and Europe takes the prize for the world’s fastest-warming continent.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: Attribution work on Europe's May heat wave found an equivalent 1976 event would have been about 3.5 °C (6.3 °F) cooler than under today's conditions, quantifying the anthropogenic contribution.
insights.so_what: A concrete attribution magnitude that can be plugged into forward heat-wave severity assumptions rather than treating events as stationary.
insights.quote: A similar heat wave in 1976 would have been about 3.5 °C (6.3 °F) cooler than it was under today’s conditions.
insights.locator: One study looked at the continent’s May heat wave
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: El Niño adds no new energy to the climate system — it redistributes heat already stored in the oceans into the atmosphere, which is why it shifts single-year temperatures without changing the long-term trend.
insights.so_what: Separates cyclical from structural warming: 2027 records would be a redistribution spike layered on trend, not evidence of trend acceleration.
insights.quote: El Niño doesn’t actually add energy into the climate system or warm up the entire globe on a long-term scale. It’s essentially just taking heat that’s been stored in the oceans and releasing it into the atmosphere.
insights.locator: And this could be a big deal for global temperatures
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: El Niño's temperature effect lags the ocean pattern by several months, and in recent events the record-breaking year has been the second calendar year of the event — 2024 became the hottest year on record from an El Niño that developed in 2023.
insights.so_what: The tradeable implication is timing: position heat-exposed risk for 2027, not for the tail of 2026.
insights.quote: The most recent El Niño developed in 2023 and ran into 2024, and 2024 is the reigning hottest year on record.
insights.locator: In some recent El Niño periods
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration defines El Niño onset as the specified part of the Pacific Ocean running 0.5 °C hotter than usual plus associated atmospheric changes, and that threshold has already been crossed.
insights.so_what: The trigger is confirmed, not forecast, which removes one layer of uncertainty from 2027 heat expectations.
insights.quote: We’ve already entered an El Niño phase, defined by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration as a period when we see the temperature in a specific part of the Pacific Ocean get 0.5 °C hotter than usual
insights.locator: We’ve already entered an El Niño phase
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: The physical mechanism is trade wind weakening: heat that normally gets pushed west builds up in the central Pacific, warming the air above it and disrupting rainfall and weather patterns globally.
insights.so_what: Global rainfall disruption, not just temperature, is the transmission channel into agricultural and hydro-power outcomes.
insights.quote: During an El Niño, the trade winds weaken and heat stored in the central Pacific builds up, warming up the air above it and creating a pocket of air that disrupts movement in the atmosphere and oceans
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: Some forecasts put this El Niño peaking at over 3.5 °C above average, which would make it the strongest on record, and Zeke Hausfather notes it had one of the fastest onsets in the observational record.
insights.so_what: A record-strength event plus multi-month lag is the specific setup for 2027 exceeding 2026 — the article's central forecast.
insights.quote: Some forecasts predict that the event could peak at over 3.5 °C above the average, potentially making it the strongest on record.
insights.locator: This El Niño is expected to be an especially notable one
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: Because climate change has loaded large amounts of heat into ocean and atmospheric storage, superimposing a strong El Niño on that stock produces outcomes worse than either factor alone would suggest.
insights.so_what: The compounding framing means historical El Niño analogs understate the expected 2027 temperature response.
insights.quote: But climate change has pushed a lot of heat into storage in the atmosphere and oceans—so combining the effects of this year-to-year variation with that long-term trend could have brutal results.
insights.locator: But climate change has pushed a lot of heat
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: UN Secretary-General António Guterres framed the event in June as El Niño conditions pouring fuel on the fire of a warming world, signaling institutional escalation ahead of 2027.
insights.so_what: High-level political framing ahead of a likely record year raises the odds of adaptation funding and policy announcements through 2027.
insights.quote: “El Niño conditions will pour fuel on the fire of a warming world,” United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in a video statement in June.
insights.locator: Given how brutal these summer heat waves have been
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: The author's concrete near-term advice is to buy an air conditioner, install solar plus a backup battery, and upgrade home insulation ahead of 2027.
insights.so_what: Direct demand-side read for residential cooling, distributed solar-plus-storage and building-envelope retrofit suppliers into 2027.
insights.quote: If you’ve been putting it off, I’d buy that air conditioner, install solar and a backup battery, or upgrade the insulation in your home.
insights.locator: It’s time to start preparing for it
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart

insights.claim: Adaptation spending does not bend the temperature path — the article is explicit that warming continues as long as fossil fuel burning continues, with mitigation framed around ending fossil fuel dependence, accelerating renewables, and universal early warning systems.
insights.so_what: Frames adaptation demand as a persistent structural growth channel rather than a one-cycle spike tied to this El Niño.
insights.quote: In the longer term, though, temperatures will keep climbing because we’re still burning fossil fuels and driving climate change.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
